title: Are/Are Tape #1 - GCPW, May 24th 1983
creator: George Coates
description:
Are Are premiered at Theatre Artaud’s Cavernous Performance Space in San Francisco in March 1983. The second part of the “How Trilogy,” it reunited Paul Dresher, Rinde Eckert, John Duykers, and Leonard Pitt, shifting from the distinct individual figures of The Way of How toward a coordinated group identity.
The performance opened with three performers hunched behind rear-lit screens, appearing as indistinct forms before emerging to measure their bodies with retractable tapes. Set on a deep, runway-like stage, the work developed around repeated attempts to measure, rise, and overcome physical limits. The performers moved in rolling barrels, climbed onto a rolling piano, appeared on stilts, and ultimately ascended in block-and-tackle harnesses with arms extended in flight. Pink and green projected patterns covered the performers as they rose. Through these successive scenes, Are Are developed a theme of ascent: the performers pool their efforts, negotiate gravity, and finally achieve lift-off

title: KQED Piece on Actual Sho, John Rozcak
creator: George Coates
description: Actual Sho (1987) was a new music theater spectacle, formed by a synthesis of familiar performance techniques with emerging ideas and technologies. The work was created through the collaboration of performers, technicians, engineers, designers, composers, architects and craftspeople from developing industries and cultural institutions in the San Francisco area. From October 1986 through June 1987 the participants met daily to pool resources and to influence each other. From these investigations a theater of phenomena is created through the interaction of talents and technology with archetypes of power; personal, political and spiritual. No single identity or individual serves as fundamental protagonist or antagonist. In Actual Sho, 'hero' is replaced by an interactive network of physical forces and human influences. Behaviors are effected through interventions of sound, light and gravity within the context o f oratorio. Performance conventions of the oratorio serve as points of departure from a form of cultural expression familiar to western audiences - the choral concert - to emerging forms of creative expression which aim to evoke, rather than provoke.

creator: George Coates
description: Box Conspiracy: An Interactive Sho (1993), premiered in San Francisco November 10, 1993. It takes its title from the impending introduction of the Digital Converter Box that will make interactive communication a possibility (perhaps even a necessity for every home television. George Coates' first character-driven production, it is the story of Derek Hornsby, an unemployed white collar professional, and his family. They are selected as a test family by a market research firm eager to learn which of the new 5,000 interactive TV channels people would use if they were free of charge. "The dark side to this," Coates says, "is that two-way television also means that without their knowledge, home users of the box will be monitored, their use of it recorded, and their service purchase records sold to marketers and insurance companies to learn everything about us."

title: 2020 Blake | August 20th 1996
creator: George Coates
description:
20/20 Blake was inspired by the life, poetry, and visual art of William Blake. Premiering in São Paulo in 1996 and receiving its North American premiere in San Francisco in 1997, the production used digitally manipulated projections of Blake’s paintings and engravings, viewed through 3-D glasses, to create an immersive stage environment in which performers appeared to move through Blake’s illuminated imagery.

Rather than presenting a linear biography, the work staged a sequence of imaginative and emotional moments from Blake’s life and visionary world. Choral performance, orchestral and rock music, dance, pantomime, projected imagery, and limited spoken text combined to translate Blake’s poetry and mythological figures—including Catherine Blake, Urizen, Thel, and Los—into a contemporary theatrical experience. The production aimed to introduce new audiences to the intensity and visual imagination of Blake’s illuminated books through an expansive, technologically experimental form of live performance.

title: The Nowhere Band | March 2, 1995
creator: George Coates
description:
Nowhere Nowhere (1994) was an immersive multimedia stage work by George Coates that combined live singing and performance with real-time computer graphics, film imagery, and stereoscopic 3-D effects. Developed through Coates’s collaborations with engineers and technology partners—including NASA Ames Research Center, Apple Computer, Intel, and the Science Meets the Arts Society (SMARTS)—the production explored how emerging digital tools could extend live theater beyond the conventional stage.

recipient:
Rare Area (1985) was a new theater work by George Coates, presented at Theater Artaud in San Francisco through January 5, 1985. It combined a rock-opera score, mime, comedy, projected imagery, and giant balloons in a sequence of visual and musical events rather than a conventional plot.

The four performers—listed as tenor, soprano, mime, and actor—moved through transient scenes and figures, including a dictator and his wife, a convict, and a woman suspended from a building. The production unfolded on a sloping platform behind several projection screens, with changing images of a Victorian San Francisco house, an ancient tomb, a tree-lined street, and patriotic imagery. In one scene, a woman falls from the projected Victorian house as two people watch from its windows. Through these episodic scenes, Rare Area addressed chauvinism and patriotism through comic and dramatic means.

SeeHear - edited selections
description:
Seehear (1983) completed the “How Trilogy” in summer 1984 at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley. Structured around the conventions of a chamber concert, the production featured a thirteen-member ensemble, conductor Roger Nelson, singers John Duykers, Rinde Eckert, and Tomasa Eckert, and mime Hitomi Ikuma.
The work began as a formal concert: musicians tuned their instruments, the conductor entered, and the audience applauded. As the overture progressed, screens and borders descended around the orchestra, forming a projected enclosure whose colors and patterns gradually covered the musicians and made them appear to dissolve into their surroundings. Singers and performers appeared high above the orchestra amid images of ancient rock carvings, while the conductor performed from a revolving tripod that allowed him to turn upside down or lie horizontally. A projected chess game appeared to float overhead. The finale transformed the expected grand operatic conclusion into a disappearing act: the orchestra continued playing as the front of the stage lowered the musicians into the pit, while the performers waved goodbye from above. Seehear closes the trilogy with an image of performers, music, projected light, and stage architecture merging into a single environment.

title: The Way of How 12 min 46 seconds
description:
The Way of How premiered at the San Francisco International Theatre Festival in September 1981 and later toured throughout the United States and Europe, including a 1983 presentation in the Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Next Wave series. It was the first work in George Coates’ “How Trilogy,” created with composer Paul Dresher, tenor singers Rinde Eckert and John Duykers, and mime Leonard Pitt.
Described by Coates as a “reverie,” the performance followed four distinct figures as they explored an environment of tubes, poles, hoops, mirrors, hand trucks, and other elemental objects. The performers transformed these materials into musical instruments, sculptural forms, and visual events: tubes became pitched percussion instruments, hoops became horns, and two descending poles appeared to carry the singers’ voices into the mime’s body. The work used operatic excerpts, musical games, monologues—including a “To B” sequence of composers whose names begin with B—and live vocal looping. Its scenes centered on discovery, tentative alliances, and the changing relationships among performers, objects, sound, and space.
